title: Fast Fashion
resolution: Resolved: The harms of fast fashion outweigh its benefits.
summary: Cheap, quickly changing clothing has made fashion affordable for many people and created millions of factory jobs, but it also creates waste and pollution. Do the harms outweigh the benefits?

background.p: **Fast fashion** is clothing designed, made and sold quickly and cheaply to follow trends, often worn only a few times. The EPA estimated that Americans generated about 17 million tons of textile waste in 2018; about 2.5 million tons (14.7%) were recycled, 3.2 million tons burned for energy, and 11.3 million tons landfilled.

Garment manufacturing employs millions of workers, many of them women, in countries such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia. Supporters of the industry, such as Johan Norberg of the Cato Institute, argue that garment exports have been a major path out of poverty, citing World Bank figures on falling extreme poverty in Bangladesh and Cambodia. Critics point to unsafe conditions (the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh killed more than 1,100 workers), low wages, water and chemical pollution, and waste exported to poorer countries. A 2018 article in *Environmental Health* (Bick, Halsey and Ekenga) described these burdens as a global environmental injustice.

disputed.q: Are garment factory jobs good for workers in poor countries?
positions: Many economists say export factory jobs pay more than the realistic alternatives and have helped reduce poverty.
Critics say wages and safety remain poor, and that progress came despite, not because of, pressure for ever-cheaper clothing.

terms.def: Trend-driven clothing produced quickly and cheaply in large volumes.
All the steps and companies involved in making and delivering a product.
Pay high enough to meet a worker's basic needs where they live.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Fast fashion's waste, pollution and worker harms outweigh the savings on cheap clothes.

args.warrant: Clothes made to be worn a few times are thrown away quickly; most end up in landfills, where synthetic fabrics break down very slowly.
args.evidence: EPA (2018): 11.3 million tons of textiles landfilled in the U.S.; research on clothing utilization.
args.response: The negative answers that waste comes from consumer habits, and recycling and resale are growing.

args.warrant: Dyeing and finishing fabrics use large amounts of water and chemicals, and much manufacturing relies on fossil fuels.
args.evidence: Bick, Halsey and Ekenga (2018) on environmental and health burdens; reports on textile dyeing pollution.
args.response: The negative replies that these harms come from manufacturing generally, and cleaner production is possible within the industry.

args.claim: Workers face unsafe conditions and low pay.
args.warrant: Pressure for speed and low prices pushes factories to cut costs, including on safety.
args.evidence: The 2013 Rana Plaza collapse; labor-rights reports on garment factories.
args.response: The negative answers that safety reforms since Rana Plaza have improved conditions, and the jobs pay more than alternatives.

args.claim: The burdens fall on poorer countries.
args.warrant: Rich countries get cheap clothes while producing countries bear the pollution, and used clothing is often shipped back to them as waste.
args.evidence: Bick and colleagues (2018) describing a global environmental injustice; reports on used-clothing exports.
args.response: The negative argues producing countries choose these industries because they bring jobs and growth.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Affordable clothing and millions of jobs are real benefits; the harms can be reduced without ending the industry.

args.claim: Garment jobs have helped lift millions out of poverty.
args.warrant: Export factories often pay more than farming or informal work, giving workers, especially women, income and independence.
args.evidence: Norberg (Cato, 2015) citing World Bank figures on poverty in Bangladesh and Cambodia; development economics research.
args.response: The affirmative answers that jobs could exist with better wages and safety; cheapness isn't required for jobs.

args.warrant: Cheap clothing lets families with tight budgets dress children for school and adults for work.
args.evidence: Consumer price data on clothing; household spending surveys.
args.response: The affirmative replies that higher-quality clothing lasts longer and can cost less over time.

args.claim: The harms can be addressed directly.
args.warrant: Safety laws, recycling programs and cleaner dyeing target the harms without ending affordable clothing.
args.evidence: Factory safety agreements after Rana Plaza; textile recycling programs.
args.response: The affirmative argues reforms have been slow, and the business model depends on volume.

args.claim: Ending fast fashion could hurt the workers critics want to help.
args.warrant: If demand falls sharply, factories close, and workers lose jobs with few better alternatives.
args.evidence: Economic studies of garment-sector employment; reports on effects of boycotts.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a gradual shift toward better production can protect jobs.

strawmen.strawman: Critics just think cheap clothes are tacky.
strawmen.why: Critics focus on waste, pollution and worker safety.
strawmen.steelman: Fast fashion's waste, pollution and unsafe conditions fall heavily on poorer countries, outweighing the savings on cheap clothes.

strawmen.strawman: Defenders don't care about factory workers.
strawmen.why: Defenders argue the jobs help workers escape poverty.
strawmen.steelman: Garment jobs have helped millions escape poverty, cheap clothing helps low-income families, and the harms can be fixed directly.

weak.arg: Everyone should just buy expensive clothes.
weak.why: Ignores families on tight budgets; it hands the other side its best argument.

weak.arg: Factories are fine now; Rana Plaza was a one-time accident.
weak.why: Dismissive and contested; argue about reforms with evidence.

aff: What jobs would garment workers have without these factories?
How would low-income families afford clothing?
Which harms could be fixed with regulation?
neg: How many tons of textiles are landfilled in the U.S. each year?
Who bears the pollution from dyeing?
